STYLE: PAINTERLY, GOUACHE IN VECTOR (for reflective, human and historical stories; wellbeing; values; moments that should feel felt)
- Paint the masses first: a clear value structure of light, middle and dark shapes, then colour with temperature shifts (warm light, cool shadow, warm bounce). Perspective is correct but drawn by hand, with no ruler-perfect edges.
- Edges are lost and found: some silhouettes dissolve into the wall behind them, others are crisp where the light hits; contours are shaped like brush strokes (tapered, slightly irregular paths), never a uniform outline.
- Gouache surface: flat, opaque strokes that follow the form, with a few dry-brush edges where a stroke runs out; detail is suggested by 2 or 3 strokes (the books on a shelf are a rhythm of coloured marks, not drawn books). Suggestion never removes structure: a chair still has its seat, back and legs in the right places.
- Simplify by distance: near objects get the most strokes, the far wall is a few broad planes.
- A limited palette per scene: at most five of the families carry the picture (the scene names them when it matters); the others appear only as small notes. Hard edges only at the focal point; edges soften toward the frame's sides. Keep each file under the size budget: fewer, larger brush strokes rather than many tiny ones.
- Light: Afternoon light painted as warm opaque strokes on surfaces it touches; shadows are cool and transparent-looking (shadow colour at 0.25 to 0.35 with brush-shaped edges); light spills and bounces (warm on the floor under the window, warm reflected light under the table edge). Direct low sun is warm; daylight that is only sky light (the room away from the sun patches) reads cool and slightly blue; lamps read orange. Keep those three apart.
- Texture: In lm-texture only, made of vector marks: brush streaks that follow surfaces (brick courses, wood grain, the weave of a rug), dry-brush flecks at stroke ends, a sparse paper grain. Dense where the light is, almost none in shadow. Never a noise overlay across the whole frame.
- Depth: Far: broad, softer, cooler, fewer strokes. Mid: full painting. Near: the boldest strokes and the warmest lights, a foreground object partly out of the frame.
- Quality bar: An illustrator's gouache painting for a thoughtful picture book or editorial cover for adults: you can feel the hand and the light, and the room still reads clearly at a glance.

THE WORLD: INSIDE THE BODY AND THE MICROSCOPIC
The inside of one healthy adult body, seen at true microscopic scale. Every set is a real tissue of the same body: the blood in a small artery, the skin on the back of a hand, the air sacs deep in the lungs, the lining of the large intestine, and a patch of the brain's outer layer. Each is drawn as a believable, softly lit place with the real shapes and the real relative sizes of what is there, simplified only by leaving out clutter: real tissue is packed far more densely than these sets show, and each scene says so.
Architecture:
- blood: red blood cells as biconcave discs about 7.5 micrometres across and about 2 micrometres thick at the rim (thinner in the dimpled centre), never spheres or doughnuts with a hole; white blood cells larger and round (a neutrophil about 12 micrometres) with a ruffled surface; platelets as small flat ovals 2 to 3 micrometres; the fluid (plasma) clear and pale straw-yellow
- vessel walls: lined with one layer of thin, flat cells (endothelium) elongated along the flow, each with an oval bulge where its nucleus sits, fitted together like long paving stones; the smallest vessels (capillaries) only 5 to 10 micrometres wide, so red cells pass in single file
- skin: the surface layer is a pavement of flat, many-sided dead cells (corneocytes) about 30 to 50 micrometres across and less than 1 micrometre thick, overlapping like roof tiles and lifting at their edges before they flake off; crossed by a diamond pattern of fine furrows; hairs about 75 micrometres thick rising from their openings with overlapping scales on the shaft; sweat duct openings about 20 to 50 micrometres across
- lungs: hundreds of millions of air sacs (alveoli), each about 200 micrometres across, opening off small ducts like the cells of a honeycomb; their walls very thin and filled with a dense net of capillaries; alveolar macrophages (cleaner cells about 20 micrometres across) crawling on the inner surface
- large intestine: a lining of tall column-shaped cells with a fuzzy top edge (the brush border), mucus-making goblet cells among them, and the openings of tube-shaped pits (crypts); above it a firm inner mucus layer, normally free of bacteria, and above that a looser outer mucus layer where the gut's bacteria live
- brain: neurons with cell bodies about 15 to 25 micrometres across, long branching dendrites studded with tiny spines (about 1 to 2 micrometres), one thin axon each, wrapped in places by a segmented fatty sheath (myelin) with small gaps; star-shaped support cells (astrocytes) touching the capillaries
Materials: wet, glossy, translucent living tissue: soft pinks, creams and reds, pale straw-yellow fluids, clear gels, a few cooler blues and violets in the brain and the lungs. Nothing is hard-edged or metallic. Palette families in this world (the set palette was named for rooms): fluids, mucus and the wet sheen on surfaces are glass; the main tissue surfaces and vessel walls are wall; a second tissue or a cell type that must read apart from the walls is fabric2; red blood cells and blood-filled capillaries are brick; white blood cells, macrophages and pale cells are paper; bacteria are plant; neurons and their branches are fabric; the deep background beyond the tissue is ceiling (for an enclosed, dark place) or sky (for an open, lit one); hair and keratin plates are wood; one small signal (a virus, a nerve impulse, a pollutant particle) is accent; a soft inner glow is light
Scale (draw to these real sizes; a person is about 1.75 m):
- 1 micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre; a human hair is about 75 micrometres thick
- a red blood cell is about 7.5 micrometres across; a capillary 5 to 10 micrometres; a neutrophil about 12; an alveolar macrophage about 20; a platelet 2 to 3
- a skin surface cell is 30 to 50 micrometres across; a common skin bacterium (a round coccus) about 1 micrometre; a gut bacterium (a rod) about 1 by 2 to 3 micrometres; a flu virus about 0.1 micrometre, too small to see at any scale used here
- an alveolus is about 200 micrometres across; a fine air pollution particle (PM2.5) is up to 2.5 micrometres
- a neuron's cell body is about 15 to 25 micrometres; a dendritic spine 1 to 2 micrometres; the colon's inner mucus layer about 100 micrometres thick (measurements range from 50 to 300)
- each scene states its own scale (pixels per micrometre) and keeps it for everything in the picture
Signs of life (every set shows someone works here):
- life in motion: cells caught mid-tumble, a white cell squeezing through a gap, bacteria dividing (one rod pinched in the middle), a cell flake lifting
- the body's work: oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood (brighter and darker red) in neighbouring vessels, mucus being made, a hair growing, a cleaner cell carrying a swallowed particle
- wear and repair: a damaged patch of lining being repaired, a skin flake curling away, a spent platelet clump
- traces from outside: a speck of dust in the lungs, a fibre of food in the gut, a smear of grime on the skin
Default light: There is no daylight inside the body. Every set uses a soft, even, warm-white light that seems to come through the thin tissue itself, brightest at the far opening or the centre of the space, so each surface shows a gentle glossy highlight on the side toward that glow and a soft translucent shade on the other; no hard cast shadows except small contact shadows where things touch.
Outside: There is no outside: each set is enclosed tissue or a space within it.
Motifs: Use at least three of these in every scene so the sets belong to one body (each scene names the ones its camera can see): biconcave red blood cells wherever blood shows, a fine capillary with red cells in single file, a wet glossy sheen on every surface, soft translucent tissue lit from within, tiny drifting specks in the fluid, the empty scale-bar slot in the lower right corner.

OBJECTS: every object must be a real, recognisable thing built the way the real one is built. A chair is
a chair at a glance and in silhouette; nothing is an invented shape, a blob or a hybrid. A style may simplify
the surface, never the parts that make an object what it is (seat, back and legs; a lid and a hinge). Build
these as described (and anything else in the set the same way: the real object, its real parts and size):
- red blood cell: a biconcave disc about 7.5 micrometres across: round in face view with a shallow dimple in the middle (darker there because it is thinner), about 2 micrometres thick at its rounded rim and about 1 micrometre at the centre, so edge-on it looks like a short dumbbell; smooth, glossy, red; no nucleus, no hole; flexible, so it bends when it squeezes past something
- white blood cell: a neutrophil about 12 micrometres across: a round, pale cream cell with a softly ruffled, slightly bumpy surface; where it touches a wall it flattens into a contact patch; through its translucent body a faint lobed nucleus (three or four connected lobes) shows
- platelet: a small flat oval about 2 to 3 micrometres long and less than 1 thick, pale straw to pale pink, smooth; a few stuck together in a small clump
- vessel lining: the inside wall of the vessel: one layer of thin, flat cells (endothelium) about 10 micrometres wide and 30 to 50 long, all elongated along the flow, fitted edge to edge like long paving stones with fine darker borders, each with a soft oval bulge where its nucleus sits; glossy and wet
- plasma: the fluid of the blood: clear and pale straw-yellow (never red), with a faint haze and a few tiny drifting specks
- scale bar: a plain horizontal line of a stated length in pixels with a short upright tick at each end, in the lower right corner, with an empty slot rect beside it for its label (no numbers drawn)
- air sac: an alveolus: a rounded, cup-shaped chamber about 200 micrometres across, open on one side to a small duct, sharing thin walls with its neighbours like the cells of a honeycomb; the walls pink, thin and translucent, with a wet film on their inner surface
- capillary net: a dense mesh of capillaries in the air sacs' walls: smooth tubes 6 to 8 micrometres wide joining and branching in a net, filled with red blood cells passing in single file and bending to fit
- alveolar macrophage: a cleaner cell about 20 micrometres across: irregular and pale, with ruffled, reaching edges and a few small dark particles visible inside it
- dust particles: fine particles of dust and soot: dark grey irregular specks 1 to 10 micrometres across (the finest, PM2.5, are up to 2.5 micrometres), some in small clumps
- airway: the end of a small airway (a bronchiole about 0.5 mm across): a round tunnel with a smooth, slightly ridged lining, darker and deeper than the air sacs
- neuron: a pyramidal neuron: a cell body shaped like a rounded pyramid 15 to 25 micrometres tall with a pale round nucleus inside; one thick main dendrite rising from its tip and branching; several thinner dendrites spreading from its base, each branching and tapering; one thin axon leaving the base
- dendritic spines: tiny protrusions 1 to 2 micrometres long along the dendrites, of three kinds: thin ones, short stubby ones and mushroom-shaped ones with a round head on a narrow neck
- axon and myelin: the neuron's single thin output fibre, about 1 micrometre thick, wrapped in places by pale, pearly sausage-shaped sheaths (myelin) with small bare gaps (nodes) between them; it branches near its end into small knobs
- synapse: the meeting point of an axon's small swollen ending and a dendrite's spine, separated by a gap too narrow to see at this scale, drawn as a hairline with a faint glow
- astrocyte: a star-shaped support cell about 20 micrometres across with many fine, branching, slightly fuzzy arms, some ending in small flattened feet pressed against a capillary
- capillary: a small blood vessel about 7 micrometres wide, a smooth translucent tube with red blood cells inside it in single file

THE SET TO DRAW: bloodstream: inside a small artery about 60 micrometres across, looking along it: red blood cells tumbling through clear straw-yellow plasma, a white blood cell rolling along the wall, platelets drifting, the vessel's paved lining curving all round (shots it serves: wide, mid; used for the stress response (adrenaline and cortisol carried in the blood), how the immune system responds to infection, oxygen delivery and fitness, vaccines, why hydration and sleep matter)
Plan (draw from it; positions in the frame below come from this camera):

- Scale at the reference depth (where the vessel's inside diameter just fills the frame's height): 1 micrometre = 18 px, so a red cell there is about 135 px across and a neutrophil about 215 px. Nearer things are larger, farther ones smaller, in true perspective.
- Real blood is crowded (red cells are about 45 percent of its volume); this set shows them far sparser, a few dozen in view, so the place reads and leaves room.

The wall's lining runs out of all four edges of the frame and recedes toward that point. A moderate wide lens: about 60 degrees across.
Composition: The vessel wall wraps the whole frame: its lining of long, flat cells (each about 10 micrometres wide and 30 to 50 long, an oval bulge at its nucleus) recedes in a paved pattern toward the far opening, a soft glowing ring at x 1150, y 470 about 120 px across. The wall is brightest near that opening and darker and redder toward the frame's edges. Red blood cells fill the lumen at three depths: two near ones, out of focus and cropped by the lower right corner (about 420 px across, x 1500 to 2100, y 760 to 1180, one face-on showing its dimple, one edge-on showing its dumbbell profile); a loose stream at the reference depth (about 135 px across) running from the lower centre up toward the opening, mostly right of centre (x 900 to 1700, y 350 to 900); and small far ones (40 px down to 15 px) converging on the opening. A white blood cell (a neutrophil, about 215 px, round with a ruffled surface and a slightly flattened contact patch) rolls along the lower left wall at x 520, y 860, a little in front of the reference depth. Six or seven platelets (40 to 50 px flat ovals) drift between the red cells. Focal point: the stream of red cells pouring toward the far opening. Free zones for narrators and mascots: (1) the open lumen left of centre from x 160 to 820, y 160 to 640, plain straw-yellow plasma against the lit wall; (2) the upper right lumen from x 1350 to 1800, y 110 to 320; no cell crosses either.
Light: No daylight: a soft warm-white glow comes from the far opening, as if light shines through the vessel ahead. Every red cell has a bright rim on its side toward the opening and a soft, translucent shade on its near face, its dimple a little darker; the white cell is pale cream with a pearly highlight. The wall's lining is lit pink-cream near the opening and falls to a deeper red toward the frame edges. The plasma is clear pale straw-yellow with a faint haze that thickens toward the opening (lm-atmos). Only tiny contact shadows where the white cell touches the wall.
Far layer: The vessel's lining all round with its paved cells, the glowing far opening, the far and reference-depth red cells and platelets, and the white cell on the wall.

Near layer: The two big out-of-focus red cells at the lower right corner (x 1500 to 2100, y 760 to 1180), cropped by the frame; they touch no free zone.

Plan (draw from it; positions in the frame below come from this camera):
- ABSTRACT (scale-free, no floor plan): a view from inside an alveolar duct into the air sacs around it; the composition is set directly in frame terms and was not plan-checked.
- Scale at the reference depth (the back wall of the central air sac): 1 micrometre = 4 px. So an air sac (alveolus) there is about 800 px across, a capillary in its wall about 24 to 32 px wide, a red cell in it about 30 px, the cleaner cell (an alveolar macrophage, about 20 micrometres) about 80 px, and a fine pollution particle (PM2.5) up to 10 px. Around it, the mouths of neighbouring sacs open like the cells of a honeycomb: one at the upper left (x -100 to 480, y -60 to 420), one at the lower left (x 60 to 520, y 640 to 1180), one at the right (x 1480 to 2060, y 260 to 840), each a darker, deeper cup. The thin walls between sacs are pink and translucent, laced with a dense net of capillaries (tubes 24 to 32 px wide at the reference depth, thicker nearer) in which red blood cells travel in single file as small biconcave discs; the net is brightest red on the central sac's back wall. A cleaner cell (an alveolar macrophage: an irregular, ruffled, pale cell about 80 px, with one dark particle inside it) crawls on the central sac's lower wall at x 860, y 770. Six to eight specks of dust and soot (dark irregular particles 4 to 10 px) float in the air in the central sac and the duct. At the upper right, the small airway that feeds this duct leaves the frame as a darker round tunnel (x 1500 to 1800, y -40 to 200). Free zones for narrators and mascots: (1) the open air inside the central sac's mouth from x 700 to 1280, y 230 to 560 (only a single dust speck there, which the narrator may cover); (2) the duct's open air at the lower right from x 1250 to 1800, y 760 to 1020.
Light: No daylight: a soft, cool white glow fills the air in the sacs, brightest at the back of the central sac, as if light comes through the thin walls. The walls are lit pink with a wet sheen and translucent edges where they are thinnest; the capillary net glows red where it faces the light. The macrophage is pale and pearly with a soft highlight on its upper ruffles. The neighbouring sacs and the airway are deeper and dimmer. A faint haze in the air (lm-atmos).
Far layer: The central sac's back wall with its capillary net, the neighbouring sacs, the airway tunnel at the upper right, and the dust specks deep in the sac.
Mid layer: The cleaner cell on the lower wall, and the dust specks near the sac's mouth.
Near layer: The thin rims of the duct's own wall at the frame's left and bottom edges, out of focus (about x 0 to 160 and y 1000 to 1080); they touch no free zone.
Motifs this camera can see (draw these; the others are out of view here): biconcave red blood cells (in the capillaries), a fine capillary with red cells in single file, a wet glossy sheen on every surface, soft translucent tissue lit from within, tiny drifting specks in the fluid, the empty scale-bar slot in the lower right corner

========== SET 3 of 3 ==========
THE SET TO DRAW: neurons: a small patch of the brain's outer layer seen up close: a few branching neurons with spiny dendrites and one long axon, a star-shaped support cell touching a capillary, and connections where an axon meets a dendrite (shots it serves: wide, mid; used for how learning and practice change the brain (spacing, retrieval, habits), sleep and memory, stress and attention, why breaks matter for focus)
Plan (draw from it; positions in the frame below come from this camera):
- ABSTRACT (scale-free, no floor plan): a view into a slab of brain tissue; the composition is set directly in frame terms and was not plan-checked.
- Scale at the reference depth (the middle neuron): 1 micrometre = 4 px. So a neuron's cell body is 60 to 100 px, a dendrite 2 to 12 px thick, a spine 4 to 8 px, the capillary about 28 px wide with red cells about 30 px.
- Real brain tissue is packed solid with cell branches; this set thins it to three neurons, one support cell and one capillary in a deep, dark space so the connections read.
Camera: A view into the tissue with a soft depth of field: the middle neuron sharp, others softer in front and behind; no strong perspective (a long lens, about 30 degrees across). The tissue's top surface (the brain's surface) runs across the top of the frame as a faint lighter band at about y 60.
Composition: The middle neuron is the focal shape: a pyramid-shaped cell body (about 90 px, its nucleus a paler round shape inside) at x 1100, y 600; its main (apical) dendrite rises straight up from the body's tip toward the surface band, branching near the top of the frame; four or five basal dendrites spread out sideways and down from its base, each branching twice and studded along its length with tiny spines like buds on a twig; its single thin axon leaves the base and runs down and to the left, wrapped in short segments of pale myelin with small gaps between them, and leaves the frame at about x 700, y 1080. A second neuron, softer and farther back, sits at the upper right (body at x 1600, y 300) with its dendrites reaching toward the first; an axon from it crosses to the middle neuron's right basal dendrite and ends in a small swollen knob touching a spine at x 1330, y 690: the synapse, with a faint glow in the narrow gap. A third neuron, nearest and out of focus, crosses the lower right corner (its body cropped by the frame, x 1700 to 2100, y 820 to 1180). A capillary crosses the left side from top to bottom in a gentle S (about 28 px wide, from x 380, y -40 to x 300, y 1120) with red cells in single file inside it; a star-shaped support cell (astrocyte) at x 560, y 520 reaches its fine branches out, two of them ending in little flattened feet on the capillary. Focal point: the synapse where the second neuron's axon meets the middle neuron's spine. Free zones for narrators and mascots: (1) the dark open space at the lower left between the capillary and the axon, from x 420 to 900, y 700 to 1000; (2) the open space at the top left from x 450 to 950, y 120 to 380 (only fine, faint branches far behind).
Light: No daylight: the neurons are drawn as softly self-lit, translucent shapes against a deep blue-violet background, as if the tissue glows faintly from within; edges brighter than centres (a rim light), the nucleus paler. The myelin segments are pale and pearly. The synapse carries one small, soft accent-coloured glow in its gap. The capillary and its red cells are dimmer, warmer reds. The far branches fade into the dark (lm-atmos).
Far layer: The deep background with faint, out-of-focus branches, the second neuron at the upper right, the capillary with its red cells, the support cell and its feet, the surface band at the top.
Mid layer: The middle neuron with its dendrites, spines and axon, and the second neuron's axon ending at the synapse.
Near layer: The third neuron, out of focus, cropped by the lower right corner (x 1700 to 2100, y 820 to 1180); it touches no free zone.
Motifs this camera can see (draw these; the others are out of view here): biconcave red blood cells (in the capillary), a fine capillary with red cells in single file, soft translucent tissue lit from within, tiny drifting specks in the fluid, the empty scale-bar slot in the lower right corner

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- airbrushed digital smoothness (perfect gradients, plastic sheen)
- a noise or grain overlay on everything
- uniform outlines
- every edge equally sharp
- muddy colour (shadows made by adding grey instead of shifting temperature)
- fiddly detail everywhere, or strident colours fighting each other
Not in this world:
- red blood cells as spheres, balls or doughnuts with a hole; bacteria with faces; viruses drawn as big spiky balls next to cells (they are about 75 times smaller than a red cell)
- neon sci-fi glow, circuitry or a cyber look
- gore: no cut flesh, no wounds, no blood spatter
- cells of the wrong size for the scene's stated scale
- real brand names, letters or numbers (the scale bar's number is a slot)
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
